newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair cautiously optimistic over N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair cautiously optimistic over N.Ireland.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair said he was cautiously optimistic about peace prospects in Northern Ireland and believed the IRA's political wing was serious about finding a solution.

"It is sensible to be cautious but we have a ceasefire in place which is good although we are not dewy-eyed about it," Blair told The Mirror in an interview on Tuesday, marking his first three months in office.
He struck an upbeat note about trying to solve one of the most intractable guerrilla conflicts of the 20th century after the Irish Republican Army called a truce earlier this month.
"That (the ceasefire), at least, is proof that there is some serious intent and desire by Sinn Fein to pursue the democratic path," Blair said.
He also singled out for praise Ulster Unionist Party leader David Trimble for not walking out of multi-party peace talks.
Trimble's party fervently wants to maintain the province's links with Britain. Sinn Fein shares the IRA's goal of wanting a united Ireland.
Blair told The Mirror "The people of Ireland desperately want a lasting political settlement and it is possible to have it because everyone knows what we need in Ulster."
In another interview with The Sun tabloid, Blair confessed that Northern Ireland had offered the biggest highs and lows of his first three months in office.
He said that the killing of two policemen by the IRA was the low spot of his premiership so far.
He was also deeply moved by the fate of children, bitterly split for decades by a sectarian divide that has spelt so much misery and taken more than 3,200 lives.
"The moment that touched me most was being in Northern Ireland and meeting the children there. It made me so sad," he said.
"Here are these children with a terrible burden of history on them. It means they don't mix in the way that normal kids do."
He invited two groups of schoolchildren -- one Protestant, the other Catholic -- to see him in London, where they spent a week and mixed together for the first time.
Blair said it was strange that Northern Ireland had given him "both my high spot and my low spot. But I've devoted a lot of time to it."
Blair's landslide election victory on May 1 raised expectations that a new government with a massive majority would be keen to give the flagging peace process some much-needed momentum.
"If we hadn't given that hope then straight away Northern Ireland could have headed towards disaster. That is why I felt we had to start moving things on so quickly."
